q: Why is a clickable div worse than a button?
A div has no keyboard focus, no button role and no Enter or Space behaviour, so keyboard and screen reader users cannot use it. A real button provides all of that for free.
Two CSS rules match the same element. How does the browser choose?
By importance (!important), then specificity (inline, then ID, then class, attribute and pseudo-class, then element), then source order: the later rule wins a tie.
Why does await fetch(url) not throw on a 404?
fetch only rejects on network failure. An HTTP error status still resolves with a Response, so you must check response.ok or the status yourself.

## Why it exists Speed is a feature people feel but rarely mention. Pages that paint quickly, respond instantly to taps and do not jump around keep users, lift conversion and rank better; pages that stall lose all three. Performance work is also notoriously misdirected: teams micro-optimize a function that takes 2 ms while a 400 KB hero image blocks the first paint, or ship a heavy framework bundle to a phone with a slow CPU and a flaky connection. The discipline is to **measure what real users experience, find the actual bottleneck, fix the biggest thing, and prevent regressions**. **Mental model:** a web page loads in three phases that map to the user's questions. *"Is it happening?"* (the first content appears), *"Is it useful?"* (the main content is visible), *"Is it usable?"* (it responds to input and stays still). Each phase has a different bottleneck: the **network** (round trips, bytes), the **browser's rendering pipeline** (what blocks painting), and the **main thread** (JavaScript that hogs the single thread that also handles input and layout). Fix them in that order, because a fast response is wasted if the browser is blocked, and a fast render is wasted if the page then freezes on the first click. {{dg:0}} ## How it works ### The critical rendering path The browser downloads HTML and parses it into the **DOM**, downloads CSS and builds the **CSSOM**, combines them into a **render tree**, computes **layout** (sizes and positions), then **paints** and **composites** layers onto the screen. Two things **block** this: **CSS** (rendering waits for stylesheets, since styles could change what is drawn) and **synchronous JavaScript** (a plain `

// BEFORE: one long task, 10,000 items processed synchronously function processAllBlocking(items, work) { for (const item of items) work(item); } // AFTER: process in ~10 ms slices, yielding so clicks and typing are handled between slices export async function processAll(items, work, sliceMs = 10) { let sliceStart = performance.now(); for (const item of items) { work(item); if (performance.now() - sliceStart > sliceMs) { await yieldToMain(); sliceStart = performance.now(); } } } // Even better for heavy CPU work: move it into a Web Worker // const worker = new Worker(new URL("./heavy.js", import.meta.url), { type: "module" }); // worker.postMessage(items); worker.onmessage = (e) => render(e.data); ``` **3) Real user monitoring with the `web-vitals` library**, sending field data to your backend with `sendBeacon` so it survives page unload: ```js import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from "web-vitals"; function send(metric) { const body = JSON.stringify({ name: metric.name, value: metric.value, rating: metric.rating, id: metric.id, page: location.pathname, nav: metric.navigationType, effectiveType: navigator.connection?.effectiveType, }); (navigator.sendBeacon && navigator.sendBeacon("/rum", body)) || fetch("/rum", { method: "POST", body, keepalive: true }); } onLCP(send); onINP(send); onCLS(send); ``` Aggregate by route and percentile (p75) in your analytics or observability tool, and alert when a route's p75 crosses a threshold. **4) A performance budget enforced in CI** with Lighthouse CI (`lighthouserc.json`): ```json { "ci": { "collect": { "url": ["http://localhost:3000/", "http://localhost:3000/pricing"], "numberOfRuns": 3 }, "assert": { "assertions": { "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }], "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 0.1 }], "total-blocking-time": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 300 }], "resource-summary:script:size": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 200000 }] } } } } ``` Lab budgets catch regressions in pull requests, while RUM tells you whether real users benefit. Try it: measure a page with and without throttling, change one thing at a time (preload the hero, then `defer` the script, then add image dimensions), and record LCP, TBT and CLS after each change so you learn which fix mattered. ## In real products - **Google, Amazon, Walmart, Akamai and many retailers** have published studies linking tenths of a second of load time to conversion and revenue; case studies on web.dev show measurable gains after improving Core Web Vitals. - **Frameworks bake these ideas in:** Next.js (image optimization, font handling, streaming, partial prerendering), Astro and Remix (islands and streaming), SvelteKit, and Nuxt all ship image, font and code-splitting helpers aimed at the Vitals. - **Image CDNs and platforms** (Cloudflare Images, Cloudinary, Imgix, Vercel and Netlify image optimization) resize, convert to AVIF or WebP, and cache at the edge automatically. - **Search engines** use Core Web Vitals as part of page experience signals, though relevance of the content matters far more; performance mostly wins you users, not rankings. - **E-commerce and media sites** manage third-party tags (ads, A/B testing, consent banners) with budgets and tag governance because they are the largest source of INP and CLS problems. - **Mobile web on low-end Android devices** is the benchmark many teams test against, since CPU speed, not just network speed, decides JavaScript-heavy pages' usability in many markets. > [!version] Checked on 2026-10-17 (secondary sources quoting web.dev): Core Web Vitals are LCP, INP and CLS with thresholds 2.5 s, 200 ms and 0.1 at the 75th percentile; INP replaced FID in March 2024; the thresholds were reported unchanged in August 2026. API details such as `scheduler.yield()` support, Speculation Rules and Lighthouse CI assertion names change over time; check MDN and the tools' documentation before depending on them. > [!pitfall] Optimizing without measuring. You can spend weeks shaving milliseconds from code that is not the bottleneck. Start with field data and a lab trace, find the largest contributor (often one image, one script or one third party), and fix that first. > [!pitfall] Lazy-loading or CSS-backgrounding the LCP image, or using client-only rendering for content that could be static. The browser discovers the resource late and the page paints late. Make the LCP element a real, eager, high-priority `` in the initial HTML. > [!pitfall] Shipping a giant JavaScript bundle and measuring only on a fast laptop. Parse and execute time dominate on mid-range phones. Check bundle composition, split by route, remove unused dependencies, and test with CPU throttling or real devices. > [!pitfall] Ignoring layout shift sources: images without dimensions, late-injected banners, ads, and web fonts swapping. Reserve space, set aspect ratios, and test with throttled networks where the shifts become visible. > [!pitfall] Letting third-party scripts run unchecked. Tag managers and widgets can double your JavaScript and add long tasks. Audit them regularly, load late and conditionally, and remove ones nobody owns. > [!security] Performance features have security edges: `preload` and `prefetch` of third-party URLs reveal user behavior and need correct `crossorigin` and CORS settings; Subresource Integrity (`integrity=`) protects third-party scripts and styles from tampering; self-hosting fonts and scripts reduces supply-chain and privacy exposure; and caching must never store personalized or authenticated responses in shared caches. > [!prod] Treat performance as an SLO: set budgets per route, collect RUM with route, device and network dimensions, alert on p75 regressions, gate pull requests with lab checks, and review the biggest offenders after each release. Fast pages decay silently as features accrete, so make regressions visible and owned. > [!cost] Performance and cost move together: smaller images and bundles cut egress and CDN bills, good cache headers and static rendering cut origin compute, and fewer third-party calls cut vendor fees. Prefer static or cached rendering where content allows, and measure the cost per thousand page views alongside the Vitals. > [!tip] Use a simple loop: measure (field and lab), find the biggest block, change one thing, remeasure. The usual winners are, in order, a right-sized and prioritized hero image, deferred or removed JavaScript, reserved layout space, and a cached, close-to-the-user response.
q: What are the three Core Web Vitals and their 'good' thresholds?
LCP (loading) 2.5 seconds or less, INP (responsiveness) 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS (visual stability) 0.1 or less, assessed at the 75th percentile of real page loads.
Why is lab data not enough to judge performance?
Lab runs use a simulated device and network, while field data (CrUX, real user monitoring) captures real devices, networks and behavior. Use lab to diagnose and field to decide.
Why should you never lazy-load the LCP image?
The browser would delay fetching it until layout, pushing back the largest paint. Make it an eager img with fetchpriority high so it is discovered and fetched early.
How do you improve INP when a click handler runs a heavy loop?
Break the work into chunks and yield to the main thread between them, defer non-urgent work until after paint, or move computation into a Web Worker, so input is handled promptly.
How do you prevent layout shift from images and ads?
Reserve space with width and height attributes or aspect-ratio, give ads and embeds fixed-size containers, and avoid inserting content above existing content.
What is a performance budget and where should it be enforced?
Limits on metrics or sizes (for example LCP under 2.5 s, route JavaScript under a set size). Enforce in CI with lab checks such as Lighthouse CI, and verify with real user monitoring.

q: Calling setCount(count + 1) three times in one click handler adds how much, and why?
Only 1. 'count' is the snapshot from this render, so all three calls compute the same value. Use setCount(c => c + 1) to add 3.
Why does Strict Mode run effects twice in development?
To surface missing or wrong cleanup: it mounts, unmounts and re-mounts to prove the effect can be torn down and set up again safely.
Why use a stable id as a list key instead of the array index?
React uses keys to match items between renders. With index keys, reordering or inserting attaches state (input text, focus) to the wrong row.
What does the AbortController cleanup in useUser prevent?
A slow response for an old id arriving after a newer request and overwriting the newer state (a race condition).
Name one thing you should compute during render instead of storing in state.
Any derived value: a filtered list, a total, a full name. Storing it creates a second source of truth that can drift.
What changes about writing useMemo and useCallback now that React Compiler 1.0 is stable?
You write plain code first and let the compiler memoize. Add manual memoization only when profiling shows a need or for a stable effect dependency.
